title: Thermal-aware kernel packing and slice consolidation for mixed-MIG GPU fleets
creator: Maya Chen
description: Reduce tail latency and token cost for mixed-MIG workloads by packing compatible model kernels into consolidated GPU slices and steering clocks based on thermal headroom. This ticket implements a runtime layer that co-locates small/short-sequence prefill decode pairs, reuses KV cache slices where safe, and applies conservative clock steering to H100/L40S/A10 fleets to avoid thermal throttling while preserving throughput.
background: We frequently see performance regressions when multiple lightweight requests (short sequences, small batch size) are scattered across MIG partitions. Each partition duplicates kernel warming and KV allocations, which increases latency and reduces GPU thermal headroom leading to clock downsteps. Previous tickets addressed kernel-selection and partition-aware scheduling, but we still see 95th percentile spikes during sustained bursts on H100 nodes in eu-west-1. This ticket focuses on co-location and thermal-aware packing rather than changing kernel implementations.
proposed_solution: 1) Add a 'slot-packing' layer in the scheduler to identify compatible requests (model size, sequence length, quantization profile, inference phase prefill vs decode) and attempt co-location into the same MIG slice when policy allows. 2) Implement a thermal headroom estimator using NVML counters and recent power/temperature trends to compute a conservative clock-steer budget per GPU. 3) Combine slot-packing with clock steering: when headroom is low, prefer packing small requests into fewer slices and lower clocks slightly to avoid abrupt throttling. 4) Add KV-cache deduplication hints so that prefill requests with identical prefixes can reuse cached tensors across co-located slices where memory layout is compatible.
tradeoffs: - Pros: Reduces kernel warmups, reduces duplicated KV allocations, smooths temperature and avoids sudden clock drops which reduce p95/p99. - Cons: Increased scheduler complexity, potential for noisy neighbor effects if packing policy is too aggressive, risk of slight throughput loss for very large batches if over-packed. Requires careful rollout with canaries and throttling thresholds. Some heuristics will be conservative initially to avoid impacting tail latency negatively.
milestones: 2026-03-05: Experiment design and perf matrix (H100/L40S/A10, MIG configs)
2026-03-10: Prototype slot-packing scheduler + NVML headroom estimator (local lab)
2026-03-12: Bench results and refine packing heuristics
2026-03-15: Open PR for scheduler changes and clock-steer integration

2026-03-27: Evaluate canary and decide on broader rollout
acceptance_criteria: p95 latency for mixed short/medium sequence workloads reduced by >= 8% versus baseline
p99 spikes reduced with fewer thermal-induced clock transitions during sustained bursts
token-cost (measured per 1M tokens) decreases by >= 4% for canary workloads
no customer-visible increase in error rate or timeouts during canary
automated telemetry and dashboards added for packing rate, headroom, and KV dedupe hits
test_plan: Microbench: synthetic short-seq (<=64 tokens) and medium-seq (<=512 tokens) mixes at varying RPS on H100/L40S/A10 with and without MIG partitioning
Load test: replay of production trace for 24h on dedicated test cluster to observe thermal trends and clock transitions
A/B canary: 5% traffic in eu-west-1 comparing current scheduler vs packing+thermal-steer, collect p95/p99/cost metrics
Safety checks: validate KV-cache correctness for dedupe scenarios and run fuzz tests to ensure no cross-request data leakage
